cards.front: What are energy substrates, and which substrate depletions are primarily responsible for exercise fatigue?
cards.back: Energy substrates are molecules that provide starting materials for bioenergetic reactions (phosphagens, glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, and amino acids). Fatigue experienced during exercise is primarily associated with the depletion of phosphagens (ATP and CP) and glycogen. Depletion of free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids rarely limits performance.

cards.front: To what extent are intramuscular creatine phosphate (CP) and ATP depleted during high-intensity exercise?
cards.back:
• Creatine Phosphate: Decreases by 50% to 70% within the first 5 to 30 seconds of high-intensity exercise and can be almost completely depleted during exhaustive work.
  • ATP: Tightly regulated for cellular survival; decreases only slightly during moderate work, but may decline by 50% to 60% during maximal exhaustion.

cards.front: How do dynamic muscle actions compare to isometric muscle actions regarding phosphagen depletion?
cards.back: Dynamic muscle actions that produce external work consume greater metabolic energy and deplete phosphagens to a significantly greater extent than static isometric muscle actions at equivalent force outputs.

cards.front: What are the precise post-exercise repletion timeframes for ATP and creatine phosphate (CP), and which pathway powers resynthesis?
cards.back:
• ATP Resynthesis: Complete resynthesis occurs within 3 to 5 minutes post-exercise.
  • CP Resynthesis: Complete resynthesis occurs within 8 minutes post-exercise.
  • Primary Pathway: Repletion is accomplished primarily through aerobic metabolism (mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation).

cards.front: How do resistance training and Type II fiber hypertrophy influence resting phosphagen stores?
cards.back: Resistance training can increase resting phosphagen concentrations in targeted muscles (e.g., triceps brachii) due to selective hypertrophy of Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers, which naturally contain higher baseline phosphagen concentrations than Type I fibers. Total phosphagen content also increases with overall muscle mass.

cards.front: What are the normal resting amounts of glycogen stored in human muscle and liver tissue?
cards.back:
• Skeletal Muscle: Stores approximately 300 to 400 g of glycogen.
  • Liver: Stores approximately 70 to 100 g of glycogen.
Resting concentrations can be elevated through both anaerobic/aerobic training and proper dietary carbohydrate intake.

cards.front: How does increasing relative exercise intensity (% VO2max) affect the rate of muscle glycogenolysis?
cards.back:
The rate of muscle glycogenolysis increases directly with relative exercise intensity:
  • 50% VO2max: 0.7 mmol·kg-1·min-1
  • 75% VO2max: 1.4 mmol·kg-1·min-1
  • 100% VO2max: 3.4 mmol·kg-1·min-1
At intensities above 60% VO2max, muscle glycogen becomes the primary energy substrate.

cards.front: What blood glucose levels lead to carbohydrate exhaustion and clinical hypoglycemia during prolonged exercise?
cards.back:
Prolonged exercise (>90 minutes) exhausts liver glycogen stores, causing blood glucose to fall:
  • Carbohydrate Exhaustion: Declines to 2.5 to 3.0 mmol/L reduce carbohydrate oxidation and trigger exhaustion.
  • Hypoglycemia: Blood glucose levels below 2.5 mmol/L result in clinical hypoglycemic reactions.

cards.front: How does high-intensity intermittent resistance training impact muscle glycogen stores?
cards.back: High-intensity resistance training can cause 20% to 60% depletion of muscle glycogen with relatively few sets. Muscle glycogen becomes the primary bioenergetic limiting factor during high-volume training, causing selective glycogen depletion in Type II muscle fibers.

cards.front: What post-exercise carbohydrate ingestion protocol optimizes muscle glycogen repletion, and how does eccentric damage affect recovery?
cards.back:
• Optimal Protocol: Ingestion of 0.7 to 3.0 g of carbohydrate per kg of body weight every 2 hours post-exercise maximizes repletion at 5 to 6 mmol/g wet muscle mass per hour during the first 4 to 6 hours.
  • Complete Repletion: Full recovery occurs within 24 hours with adequate carbohydrate intake.
  • Eccentric Component: High eccentric muscle damage requires more than 24 hours for complete repletion due to structural microtrauma.
